sentences.text: Cretornis was a pterosaur with a wingspan estimated between 1.5 and 1.6 meters, based on a humerus approximately 3 inches long.
A unique derived trait of this animal is that the distal part of its humerus has a diamond-shaped cross-section.

Fossils were discovered in 1880 by quarry workers in Zářecká Lhota, Czech Republic, who were extracting gravel for road repair, and a local resident named Mrs. Tomková alerted pharmacist and collector František Hlaváč to the find.
Professor Antonín Frič originally identified the fossils in 1881 as a toothed bird the size of a swan and named the species Cretornis hlavaci, with the specific name honoring the collector.

Scientists later realized that the fossils originally identified as a bird actually belonged to a pterosaur, and the known fossil material consists of a partial skeleton lacking a skull, including a complete humerus, ulna, radius, wrist, and two wing finger phalanges, which are now housed in the National Museum in Prague.
In the nineteenth century, Cretornis was classified as a species within the genus Ornithocheirus.

A 2018 analysis by Nicholas Longrich and colleagues placed Cretornis within the family Nyctosauridae, a position that contradicts its placement within Azhdarchoidea, though detailed comparisons of wing bones suggest it belongs to a non-azhdarchid azhdarchoid, likely a member of the group Neoazhdarchia.
Cretornis is likely more advanced than the Thalassodromidae and shares several features with Montanazhdarcho.
Cretornis lived approximately 92 million years ago during the Turonian stage of the Late Cretaceous in what is now the Czech Republic, with a time range estimated from 93.9 to 89.8 million years ago.
